Predictive Directed Association: Information Refinement and Incremental Predictive Value. Kaining Wang manuscript How much predictive value is gained when an information set is refined? Many predictive- dependence frameworks emphasize whether additional information provides statistically de- tectable predictive improvement, while the magnitude of the resulting predictive value can be treated as a primary mathematical object in its own right. This paper develops Predictive Directed Association (PDA) from this perspective. For nested information sets, PDA is defined as the expected squared distance between the corresponding Bayesoptimal predictors. We prove that this quantity exactly equals the reduc- tion in Bayes-optimal prediction risk obtained by incorporating the richer information set in place of the baseline information set. Thus, PDA is simultaneously a probabilistic quantity, a projection distance, and a decision-theoretic measure of incremental predictive value. We establish a mathematical foundation consisting of nonnegativity and boundedness, a structural characterization of zero association, information monotonicity, an exact chain rule for nested information refinements, decision-theoretic monotonicity, and estimation stability. We further derive a conditional orthogonal decomposition and develop a dynamical-state-conditioned extension in which predictive value is evaluated within specified dynamical states. An exact construction demonstrates an important phenomenon: global predictive association can vanish completely while predictive value remains strictly positive within every state. This provides a rigorous witness that marginal predictive analysis can conceal stateconditioned predictive structure. For statistical implementation, we develop a blocked estimation framework under geomet- rically mixing observations and establish consistency and rate-transfer results under explicit empirical-process and nonparametric estimation conditions. The resulting framework is model- agnostic at its theoretical core and does not require linearity, Gaussianity, or a specific dynamical model. Rather than proposing a pointwise replacement for existing predictive-dependence measures, PDA takes information refinement and incremental predictive value as its primitive objects. This viewpoint provides a common mathematical interface connecting conditional expectation, statistical decision theory, predictive dependence, state-conditioned analysis, and nonparamet- ric estimation, while opening a route toward broader theories of decision value, distributional predictive value, and general information value

Predictive Directed Association in Dynamical-State Systems: L2 Hilbert-Space Specialization. Kaining Wang manuscript We specialize the Predictive Directed Association (PDA) framework to mean-squared-error risk on L2 space in dynamical-state systems. For MSE loss, incremental predictive risk reduction admits an exact representation as the squared L2 norm of an orthogonal-projection increment. We develop the dynamical-state apparatus: state-conditional PDA and the exact decomposition which follows from the tower property. We establish nine fundamental properties and three core theorems, all conditioned on the dynamical state ξt, including the Bayes risk equivalence, con- sistency, and rate-transfer results for empirical estimators. Under explicitly stated Riccati-style contraction hypotheses combined with geometric β-mixing, we derive sufficient conditions for exponential decay of state-conditional residuals. The I-K Dynamic Theory : A Mathematical Framework for the Interest-Knowledge Principle. Sinan Ibaguner manuscript This paper develops a formal model of the relationship between interest and knowledge. Its starting point is Sinan Ibaguner's proposed Interest-Knowledge Principle: Without Interest, There Is No Active Knowledge. The paper argues that this statement requires a distinction between information, knowledge, understanding, and active knowledge acquisition. A mathematical framework is introduced in which interest is represented as a continuous state variable that influences attention, inquiry, learning, and subsequent interest. The model includes a set of definitions, axioms, propositions, and a dynamic system. Interest is represented by I t , attention by A t , inquiry by Q t , and knowledge by K t. The framework proposes that interest may facilitate learning without being a logically necessary or sufficient condition for all forms of knowledge. A central result of the proposed theory is the distinction between a universal epistemic claim and a dynamic learning hypothesis. The former cannot be established merely through formal notation
itens.autor: The latter can be investigated through mathematical analysis and empirical research.

Commentary on Matt Duncan *Present to the Mind: Acquaintance and Its Significance*. Adam Pautz manuscript I very much enjoyed Matt Duncan’s elegant and innovative book (and also have benefited from our many discussions of these issues with him over the years). I agree with Matt Duncan about something important: experience matters. Conscious experience is one of the things that has genuine epistemic, aesthetic, and moral significance. But I disagree with him about something fundamental to his book — namely, why experience matters. On Matt’s acquaintance-based account, the significance of experience always derives from acquaintance with existing items — even in the case of hallucination. In this he follows a tradition running through Russell and Fumerton. It is the central claim of the book. On my own acquaintance-free account, by contrast, experience is fundamentally intentional: its significance is grounded in how things seem, not in acquaintance with any existing item. Here I side with Pryor, Siegel, and Smithies, among others. My comments proceed in three parts. First, I present a traditional argument from hallucination for an acquaintance-free account of the epistemic significance of experience. Second, I consider Matt’s objections to such an account, and offer my replies. Third, I ask whether this “in house” disagreement really matters — and confess that I am not sure it does
